rows.question: If a retail tenant adds a small café kitchen, what determines whether we need a grease hood?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

If a retail tenant adds a small café kitchen, what determines whether we need a grease hood?

Research complete
00:37

The cooking appliances and what they emit—not the café’s size—determine whether a Type I grease hood is required. NYC requires a Type I hood where cooking produces grease or smoke, and over medium-, heavy-, or extra-heavy-duty appliances (MC § 507.2). A narrow exception applies to an electric appliance if an approved testing agency documents grease in its effluent at no more than 5 mg/m³ when tested at 500 cfm under UL 710B. Heat or moisture without grease or smoke may instead trigger Type II hood requirements, subject to the stated HVAC or separate-removal-system exception (MC § 507.3).

To determine the result for this café, identify the appliances and cooking methods, including whether any appliance is electric and has the required test documentation. What equipment and cooking methods are planned?

What appliances and cooking methods are planned, and is any electric appliance supported by the specified UL 710B test documentation?

rows.question: For a gas boiler in the proposed building, can we run steel gas piping outdoors along the rear wall? What protection should the detail show?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

For a gas boiler in the proposed building, can we run steel gas piping outdoors along the rear wall? What protection should the detail show?

Research complete
01:11

Yes, conditionally: an exposed outdoor steel gas-piping run along the rear wall is permitted under the supplied 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code provisions, provided it meets the outdoor installation and corrosion-protection requirements and does not interfere with normal operation of windows, doors or other exit openings (FGC §§ 404.9, 404.3).

The detail should show:

Elevation and exposure: piping at least 3½ inches above ground, not concealed (FGC § 404.9).
Corrosion protection: exposed exterior steel protected by galvanizing, bonded coating complying with § 404.11.4, protective coating complying with § 404.11.5, or protective wrapping complying with § 404.11.6. Wrapping must be approved for the application and field-applied according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Protect susceptible metallic fittings and joints as well (FGC §§ 404.11, 404.11.2, 404.11.6). The supplied evidence does not include §§ 404.11.4–404.11.5, so it does not establish the specifications needed to approve either coating option.
Identification: yellow labels marked “Gas” in black, complying with ASME A13.1, at intervals no greater than 5 feet; where a gas test is required, label before testing. Marking is not required for pipe in the same room as the appliance served (FGC § 401.5).
Exterior-wall passage, if included: corrosion protection under § 404.11. If encased in a protective pipe sleeve, seal the annular space and provide at least one end with a vented outlet piped to a safe outdoor location. The terminal must be at least 18 inches above grade, not beneath a building opening or overhang, and installed to prevent water and insect entry (FGC § 404.9).

A fire-rated rear wall does not, by itself, prohibit piping on its exterior face. Piping within a required fire-rated wall or assembly is prohibited; through-penetrations must comply with BC Chapter 7 (FGC § 404.3). The secure-support and physical-damage-protection clause in the supplied § 404.9 applies to piping installed above ground, outdoors, across roof surfaces; it is not a stated requirement for this wall-mounted route.

rows.question: Could a café tenant keep propane cylinders outside this building? What fire-safety restrictions should we check before drawing a storage cage?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

Could a café tenant keep propane cylinders outside this building? What fire-safety restrictions should we check before drawing a storage cage?

Research complete
01:38

Only conditionally—not simply by placing cylinders in an outdoor cage. For the proposed mixed-use building with residential space, LPG containers larger than 16.4 ounces are prohibited anywhere on the lot unless authorized by the commissioner. Outdoor LPG storage facilities must also be approved. Thus, a typical larger-cylinder café installation is not established as permissible without that authorization and storage approval. (2022 NYC Fire Code, current consolidated text, §§ 6105.3(3), (5), 6109.1.)

Before laying out the cage, check these restrictions:

Cylinder and total quantity limits: No individual LPG container may have capacity greater than 100 pounds. Outdoor storage is limited to 400 pounds of LPG. A permit is required when quantities exceed those in FC § 105.6; that threshold text was not supplied, so the permit trigger cannot yet be determined. Approval does not settle that separate permit question. (FC §§ 6105.3(1), (4), 6109.12.)
Basic location: Storage must be at or above grade, not on a roof, and at least 20 feet from building openings, 20 feet from motor-vehicle fuel dispensers, and 10 feet from combustible material. These outdoor separation requirements include containers connected for use. (FC §§ 6109.6, 6109.12.)
Additional exposure distances: For storage of more than 100 pounds through 400 pounds, Table 6109.12 requires, where those exposures exist, 10 feet from combustible buildings or structures; 25 feet from subway openings and Group A occupancies/public gathering places; 5 feet from air-compressor intakes or HVAC inlets; and 10 feet from public sidewalks, parked vehicles, public streets, private roads and lot lines. Other table rows address nearby liquid, gas, oxygen and solid-material storage. Only distances marked with note “a”—including the public-street/private-road/lot-line row—may be reduced to 5 feet using a protective structure rated at least 2 hours that interrupts the container-to-exposure line of sight, stands at least 5 feet from the exposure, and allows natural ventilation to prevent hazardous gas accumulation. This is not a general reduction of the building-opening or other unmarked clearances. (FC Table 6109.12, note a.)
Egress and failure hazards: Do not store or leave cylinders unattended near exit-access doors, exits, stairs, exit-discharge areas or other egress areas. Do not locate storage where failure of structures or containment systems could expose the LPG to electric power lines or piping carrying flammable/combustible liquids, flammable gases or oxidizing materials. (FC §§ 6109.4, 6109.12.1.)
Enclosure and cylinder protection: Provide a suitable enclosure or other tamper protection, minimize physical damage and excessive temperature rise, and provide vehicular protection as required by the commissioner. Stored cylinders must have securely installed screw-on valve caps or collars and closed outlet valves, whether full, partially full or empty. Cylinders over 1 pound must be positioned with the relief valve communicating directly with the vapor space. (FC §§ 6109.2, 6109.3, 6109.8, 6109.13.)
Electrical equipment: Except as otherwise provided in NFPA 58, electrical equipment within 3 feet in any direction must meet Class I, Division 2 wiring requirements unless separated from the area by a wall or solid partition without openings. The supplied packet does not include the NFPA 58 alternative. (FC § 6109.14.)

If these cylinders will supply a stationary café installation, access to utility piped natural gas prohibits that LPG installation unless the commissioner authorizes it; the appliance must also be approved for LPG. A storage cage alone does not establish permission to operate the café equipment. (FC §§ 6105.1, 6105.3(10).)

The layout remains conditional on the proposed cylinder capacities, total LPG quantity, measured exposure distances and commissioner authorization. What cylinder size and total LPG quantity does the café propose?

No. The old record’s zero apartments describes the existing property, not the proposed new building. It cannot establish that no residential parking is needed for the new apartments.

If the lot is within the Inner Transit Zone, no accessory off-street parking is required for the proposed new dwelling units under the rule for units created after December 5, 2024 (ZR § 25-211). “Created” means issuance of a temporary certificate of occupancy, or a final certificate if no temporary certificate was issued. That would be the basis for no required residential parking—not the old apartment count. Your supplied Appendix I transit-zone status does not establish Inner Transit Zone status from the text provided, so that geographic applicability remains unresolved.
